missions.title: A realistic delivery date
paragraphs: A team promises a report by Friday. One required source will not be ready until Monday. The people involved need enough information to choose a practical response.

It would be helpful to explain the dependency before confirming a final date. The expected benefit is that the recipient can plan with a realistic expectation. This gives the response a clear purpose that can be checked afterwards.

Before proceeding, the people involved should check that they share the same understanding. If the first response does not resolve the problem, they can review the result and consider a different option. A clear explanation makes the next decision easier.

A deadline is useful only when people understand what must be ready by that time. A first draft, a finished document and an approved version are not the same thing. Checking the expected result helps you make a realistic promise. If a delay becomes likely, an early update gives other people more choices than a last-minute explanation.

In a similar conversation, you could say: “When do you need it by, and is a draft enough?” “I'm working on it and can send an update this afternoon.” “Could I have a little more time to check the figures?”

A report should help its reader understand something or make a decision. Including every detail can make that harder rather than easier. To avoid further confusion, we decide to check the sources and explain the discrepancy. The expected benefit is that the report can present a consistent account. This gives the response a clear purpose that can be checked afterwards.

A useful decision takes account of the information available at the time. If an important detail changes, it may be sensible to review the plan. Explaining the reason for the decision helps other people understand when a different approach might be needed.

missions.title: A useful executive summary
paragraphs: A long report is ready for review. The decision-maker has limited reading time. The people involved need enough information to choose a practical response.

One practical option is to summarise the finding and required decision at the beginning. The expected benefit is that the reader can identify the main point quickly. This gives the response a clear purpose that can be checked afterwards.

The people involved can make progress by separating the immediate action from questions that still need an answer. This prevents an incomplete explanation from becoming an unrealistic promise. A brief follow-up can establish whether the proposed response actually helped.

A report should help its reader understand something or make a decision. Including every detail can make that harder rather than easier. The main finding needs clear support, and any uncertain information should be identified. A short summary is useful when it tells the reader what matters and where to look for more detail.

In a similar conversation, you could say: “The main point is that the two totals need checking.” “Let me put it another way: we need a clearer comparison.” “As far as I can tell, the report uses last month's figures.”
